planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained volcanic soil in partial shade; K7 is a tall, frost-tender traditional Kenyan cultivar best grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: K7 was selected in Kenya from French Mission coffee stock tracing back to Bourbon, making it one of the traditional tall Kenyan cultivars alongside SL28 and SL34. It shows useful partial resistance to coffee berry disease and some leaf rust races that its more famous SL siblings lack, though yields run lower than newer compact hybrids. The tree grows tall and vigorous with a spreading habit, producing the bright, wine-toned acidity and floral aromatics characteristic of high-grown Kenyan arabica. Best suited to well-drained volcanic soils at elevation, with the same partial shade and rich organic feeding regime that suits other highland Kenyan varieties.

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Parainema is a dwarf, frost-tender Sarchimor-type hybrid best grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Bred by IHCAFE in Honduras from a cross between Villa Sarchi and Hibrido de Timor, Parainema belongs to the Sarchimor family and carries strong resistance to coffee leaf rust inherited from its Timor parent. Unlike many rust-resistant hybrids that sacrifice cup quality for disease resistance, Parainema has earned specialty-grade recognition when grown at good elevation, a legacy of the well-regarded Villa Sarchi side of its parentage. The plant stays compact and dwarf, similar in stature to Caturra, which lets growers set trees closer together and increase yield per hectare on the medium-altitude farms across Honduras, Nicaragua, and El Salvador where it now thrives. Grow it as other dwarf Central American arabica selections, with rich, well-drained acidic soil and dappled shade.

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; IHCAFE 90 is a dwarf, frost-tender rust-resistant hybrid best grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Released by the Instituto Hondureno del Cafe, IHCAFE 90 is a pedigree selection combining Hibrido de Timor with Caturra, giving it the same rust-resistant lineage as other Sarchimor and Catimor-type hybrids. It is a dwarf, high-yielding plant well adapted to the lower-elevation farms common in Honduras, where many traditional tall varieties struggle with disease pressure, though its cup profile, typically balanced, citrusy, and mild, trails behind flavor-forward heirloom varieties. Growers who take it to higher elevations and process it carefully can coax out noticeably better sweetness and clarity than the variety's reputation as a yield-focused workhorse might suggest. Culture follows other dwarf Central American arabica hybrids: rich, well-drained acidic soil, partial shade, and steady moisture.

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Costa Rica 95 is a dwarf, frost-tender high-yield hybrid best grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Developed through pedigree selection by the Instituto del Cafe de Costa Rica (ICAFE) from a cross between Hibrido de Timor and Caturra, Costa Rica 95 is a compact, conical-shaped tree with short branches, reddish-bronze new growth, and red ripe fruit. It was bred primarily for high productivity rather than lasting disease immunity, and field evaluations have shown its early rust resistance can decline over time in some growing regions, so growers still need an active disease-management program. The dwarf habit allows dense planting and it responds strongly to fertilizer inputs, rewarding well-managed farms with heavy yields. Grow it like other Central American dwarf arabica hybrids, in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with partial shade.
sources: Instituto del Cafe de Costa Rica (ICAFE)

planting.note: Establish tissue-cultured or grafted plantlets in spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Milenio is a vigorous F1 hybrid, frost-tender, best grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Milenio is an F1 hybrid variety created by cooperative Central American coffee research programs from a cross between a Sarchimor-derived line and the Ethiopian landrace Rume Sudan, part of a wave of F1 coffee hybrids bred for vigor and climate resilience rather than being fixed, true-breeding lines. It combines coffee leaf rust resistance with tolerance of coffee berry disease, strong yields, and a distinctive cup noted for dark chocolate, cane sugar, and citrus notes that exceed what older rust-resistant hybrids typically offer. Because it is an F1 hybrid, seed-grown plants show more variability than clonally propagated varieties, so commercial plantings are usually established from tissue-cultured or grafted plantlets rather than open-pollinated seed. It performs best in shaded agroforestry systems at higher elevation, and otherwise wants the same rich, well-drained, partially shaded conditions favored by other highland arabica.
sources: CATIE (Centro Agronomico Tropical de Investigacion y Ensenanza)

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich volcanic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Anacafe 14 is a vigorous, frost-tender rust-resistant hybrid best grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Anacafe 14 originated as a chance cross between Catimor and Pacamara discovered by a Guatemalan farmer and was released commercially by ANACAFE, the country's national coffee association. It inherits coffee leaf rust resistance and drought tolerance from its Catimor parent while retaining more of the Pacamara side's large bean size and cup complexity than most rust-resistant hybrids manage. Grown at higher Guatemalan elevations it can produce a surprisingly structured, sweet cup, helping shift the reputation of rust-resistant varieties away from flat or woody flavors. It grows as a vigorous, moderately sized tree and appreciates the same rich volcanic soil, partial shade, and consistent moisture as other Guatemalan highland arabicas.

planting.note: Plant seedlings or grafted plants in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; TSH 565 is a frost-tender Trinidad Selected Hybrid best grown outdoors only in zones 10-11, and requires a compatible cross-pollinator tree to set full pod loads.

directions: TSH 565 is one of the Trinidad Selected Hybrids bred at Trinidad's cacao research station from a cross of SCA 6 and ICS 1, combining a witches'-broom and black-pod-tolerant parent with a classic Trinitario flavor line. Fermentation studies have shown it develops a full, traditional chocolate flavor profile through the action of its own indigenous microbiota, and it has been adopted well beyond Trinidad, including on estates in Brazil and the Andes. Unlike some self-compatible cacao clones, TSH 565 requires cross-pollination from a genetically compatible partner tree to set a full pod load, so orchard planning should include compatible neighboring clones. Give it the warm, humid, shaded understory conditions and rich, well-drained soil that all fine-flavor cacao selections need.
sources: Cocoa Research Centre, University of the West Indies, Trinidad

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Carenero Superior is a frost-tender regional Venezuelan Trinitario cacao type best grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Carenero Superior takes its name from the small Venezuelan port on the Barlovento coast east of Caracas, where Trinitario trees carrying a strong strain of native Criollo blood have been grown for centuries. The fermented beans are prized by fine chocolate makers for a rounded, mellow chocolate base layered with notes of caramel, dried fruit, and light florals, with less astringency than many other Trinitario-type cacaos. Trees are typically grown in the humid, shaded coastal lowlands under taller shade canopy, following the same cultivation needs as other Venezuelan fine-flavor cacao. It is traded and blended as a distinct regional bean type rather than propagated under a single registered clone name, so seed and budwood sources vary by farm.
sources: International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) fine flavor cacao list

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Rio Caribe is a frost-tender regional Venezuelan Trinitario cacao type best grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Named for the colonial port town on Venezuela's Paria Peninsula where it has been grown and traded since colonial times, Rio Caribe is a Trinitario-type cacao descended from local Criollo stock and ranks among the most sought-after fine-flavor beans in the world. Its fermented, dried beans are known for deep chocolate intensity paired with nutty, low-acid, faintly coffee-like undertones rather than the brighter fruit notes typical of many other Venezuelan cacaos. The trees grow in the humid coastal lowlands of eastern Venezuela, traditionally beneath mixed shade canopy alongside other food crops in small-holder plots. As with Carenero, Rio Caribe is primarily a regional trade designation rather than a single registered clone, so plant material is typically sourced as regional seed or budwood.
sources: International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) fine flavor cacao list

planting.note: Train stem cuttings onto rough-barked trees, cork slabs, or a shaded trellis in partial shade with high humidity and moist, well-drained organic medium; Vanilla odorata is one of the wild parent species behind Vanilla x tahitensis, native from southern Mexico through Central America into tropical South America, and is only lightly cultivated for local vanilla use in Oaxaca. Source only nursery-propagated material, as wild populations are assessed as endangered.

directions: Vanilla odorata is a climbing, hemi-epiphytic orchid native to humid forests from southern Mexico through Central America and into tropical South America, best known as one of the two wild parent species, alongside Vanilla planifolia, behind the polyploid hybrid Vanilla x tahitensis grown commercially in Tahiti. It has never developed into a major commercial crop on its own, but is occasionally grown in Oaxaca as a local, small-scale source of fragrant pods used much like V. planifolia. The vine climbs by aerial roots onto rough bark or a support structure, producing pale, short-lived flowers that must be hand-pollinated within hours of opening to set pods reliably in cultivation. Because wild populations are considered endangered from habitat loss, cultivated plants should always be sourced from legitimate nursery or research-institution propagations rather than wild collection.
sources: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
Kew Royal Botanic Gardens, Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Train stem cuttings onto rough-barked trees, cork slabs, or a shaded trellis in partial shade with high humidity and moist, well-drained organic medium; Vanilla bahiana is a Brazilian native species closely related to Vanilla planifolia, restricted to the Atlantic Forest of Bahia. Source only nursery-propagated material, as wild populations are assessed as endangered.

directions: Vanilla bahiana is a climbing, hemi-epiphytic vanilla orchid restricted to the Atlantic Forest of Bahia in eastern Brazil, closely related to the commercially dominant Vanilla planifolia but never domesticated as a food crop. Its cured pods carry an earthier, drier, more resinous and smoky aromatic character than Madagascar-type vanilla, which has drawn interest from perfumers rather than confectioners, and Brazilian researchers have begun studying it as a potential source of heat- and disease-tolerant genes for vanilla breeding programs. In cultivation it climbs rough bark or a shaded support by aerial roots much like other wild Vanilla species, with short-lived flowers that need hand pollination to set pods reliably away from native pollinators. Because remaining populations are assessed as endangered due to Atlantic Forest habitat loss, cultivated material should come only from legitimate botanical-garden or research propagations.
sources: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
Kew Royal Botanic Gardens, Plants of the World Online
